newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durables orders surge gives 1997 strong start.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durables orders surge gives 1997 strong start.

text.p: Orders for long-lasting durable goods rose more strongly than expected in January, the government said Thursday, pointing to steady economic growth at the start of 1997.
The Commerce Department said that orders for cars, computers and goods meant to last three years or more jumped 3.6 percent after falling 1.8 percent in December and 1.7 percent in November.
Analysts said orders were strong across the board, pointing to solid momentum in the industrial sector, especially since backlogs also strengthened and shipments of finished products rose.

"This isn't a one-time deal," economist Kevin Flanagan of Dean Witter Reynolds Inc. in New York said. "It's reinforcing the notion of a solid growth setting, as you had gains pretty well across the board."
The rise was more than twice the 1.5 percent increase that Wall Street economists had forecast.

The report initially rocked the bond market on worries it might persuade Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan to raise interest rates a day after he said an increase might be needed to keep inflation in check.
Treasury bond prices, especially sensitive to inflation concerns, fell sharply on the news but later stabilised and the 30-year Treasury bond was modestly lower in afternoon trading.

Greenspan told Congress on Wednesday the central bank might act pre-emptively to curb inflation as the economy approaches six years of unbroken growth next month. The last recession ended in March 1991.

The Labour Department said separately that claims for jobless benefits rose 11,000 to 316,000 last week. But the four-week moving average of claims, which smooths out weekly variations, fell to its lowest level in six months at 313,250, a clear sign of steady job growth.

In its report, the Commerce Department said the strongest gain came in orders for electronic and electrical equipment, up 14.9 percent after declines of 14.1 percent in December and 10.3 percent in November.

The department said communications and electronic components accounted for most of the gain. Analysts said beforehand that computer demand was steady but noted communications equipment orders were often volatile.

Orders for transportation equipment rose 1.2 percent after a 0.9 percent fall in December. The department said more demand for new cars and parts and for commercial aircraft offset weaker orders for ships and military tanks.
Gordon Richards, an economist for the National Association of Manufacturers, said stronger durable-goods orders implied continuing gains in capital spending in 1997 to expand output.

"Coming in the wake of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's hints in yesterday's testimony that he might raise interest rates, the increase in durable goods orders may create the impression that the economy is growing too fast," Richards said.

But he added that more capital investment spending contains inflation by making it possible for manufacturing industries to produce more with the same number of employees by using newer, more efficient machinery.
John Welch, chairman of General Electric Co., which manufactures goods from aircraft engines and turbines to light bulbs, expressed similar sentiments at a session of corporate leaders on Wednesday.
Welch told the Business Council that rising productivity was being ignored as a factor curbing inflation.
"We can easily handle more growth on the industrial side without inflation," he told a news conference. "There is no inflation anywhere."
Defence orders fell 23.7 percent after falling 8.0 percent in December. Orders for primary metals rose 5.5 percent after a 4.9 percent rise.
